props.title: Wild at Heart
props.initialSlug: David Lynch's violent romance road movie

sections.content: David Lynch's Wild at Heart blazes across the screen like a fever dream road movie on acid. Nicolas Cage and Laura Dern ignite as Sailor and Lula, star-crossed lovers fleeing through a hyper-stylized American South that feels lifted from both Elvis movies and horror films. Lynch weaves The Wizard of Oz (1939) references throughout, but twisted through his signature surrealist lens. The film marked a pivotal moment in Lynch's career, coming between Blue Velvet (1986) and Twin Peaks (1990-1991), when his particular brand of darkness-beneath-the-surface storytelling crystallized into something uniquely dangerous and seductive.

sections.content: The film's influence rippled through 1990s cinema, inspiring a wave of violent romance road movies. True Romance (1993) and Natural Born Killers (1994) both owe clear debts to Lynch's fever-dream style and lovers-against-the-world narrative. Willem Dafoe's Bobby Peru remains one of cinema's most unsettling villains, establishing a template for the charismatic psychopath that would become a 90s crime film staple, echoed in characters like Gary Oldman's Drexl in True Romance (1993).

Lynch's use of music in Wild at Heart revolutionized how directors approached soundtracks. The way he weaves heavy metal with Angelo Badalamenti's dreamy score created a template followed by films like Lost Highway (1997) and Natural Born Killers (1994). The Elvis references, with Cage's Sailor repeatedly breaking into song, prefigured the post-modern musical moments that would become common in films like Pulp Fiction (1994) and Everyone Says I Love You (1996). movies.title: Mulholland Drive
movies.slug: Lynch's surreal masterpiece about Hollywood dreams and nightmares

sections.content: Wild at Heart marks a crucial transition in Lynch's filmmaking, bridging his more narrative-driven early work like Blue Velvet (1986) with the pure surrealism of later films like Lost Highway (1997) and Mulholland Drive (2001). The film's dream sequences and reality-bending moments push beyond traditional storytelling while maintaining just enough plot coherence to keep audiences engaged. This balance would become increasingly abstract in Lynch's later work.
